topic: fermenting a barrel of bittersweet cider through winter, racking it off the lees and bottling

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-3)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: areometr (hydrometer) do odczytu cukru

base: I pressed a ton of bittersweet apples last week and the juice is now in a barrel.
An older barrel sits beside it, holding cider from last autumn that has cleared beautifully.
I bought a hydrometer in the spring, since guessing at sugar levels never ended well before.
The new juice has begun to work already, though the shed is cold at night.
Should I let it ferment where it stands, or move the barrel somewhere warmer indoors?
Leave it in the cold, because a slow ferment gives cider far more flavour than a fast one.
Warmth drives the yeast hard and blows off the very aromas you pressed for.
A cold shed will keep the working gentle right through the winter months.
Fit an airlock now, and take a reading before the sugar falls too far.
I fitted an airlock and the barrel has been bubbling steadily for about nine days.
The hydrometer showed ten sixty at pressing and reads ten twenty this morning.
A thick brown scum has risen through the bung hole and run down the stave.
Is that scum a fault, or does it belong to a healthy ferment?
That brown head is normal, and throwing it out of the bung is exactly right.
Keep the barrel topped up so the scum carries clear instead of falling back in.
Wipe the stave each morning, or the dried residue will taint the wood over time.
Once the head stops rising, bung the barrel loosely and let the ferment finish quietly.
The head fell away last week and the hydrometer now reads ten oh two.
I bunged the barrel loosely and the bubbling has slowed to one every minute.
The older barrel beside it tastes much drier and rather sharper than I expected.
Should I rack this batch off the lees now, or wait until the spring?
Rack it now, because cider left long on heavy lees picks up a dull, yeasty edge.
Siphon carefully from the side, and stop the moment the run begins to cloud.
Fill the fresh barrel right to the bung, since air is the real enemy now.
A second, lighter ferment will follow in the spring and clear the cider further.
I racked the cider into a clean barrel and lost very little to the lees.
It tastes rough and still carries a faint prickle on the tongue.
Some neighbours add sugar at this stage, others insist that good fruit needs nothing.
Which course suits a barrel pressed entirely from bittersweet apples off old standard trees?
Add nothing, because bittersweet fruit carries all the body a good cider needs.
Sugar added now simply raises the strength and thins whatever character the apples gave.
That prickle is dissolved gas and will fade once the barrel warms in spring.
Roughness at this stage means very little, since tannin softens over the first year.
I left the cider alone and the prickle has indeed gone as the shed warmed.
It is clearing from the top down and tastes far rounder than it did.
I would like to bottle some in June for drinking at the harvest supper.
Is bottling straight from the barrel safe, or must something be done first?
Take a reading first, because any sugar left will work again inside a sealed bottle.
If it sits at ten hundred or below, the cider is dry and safe to bottle.
Use stout bottles either way, and keep the first few somewhere you can watch them.
A cellar that stays cool through June will hold the cider well until autumn.
